sentences.text: Protoavis is typically illustrated as a two-legged archosaur, resembling poposaurids and rauisuchids from the same era.
Its skull features an extremely narrow parietal bone and very broad, T-shaped frontals that create lateral wings where postorbitals are missing.
In contrast, the well-preserved wrist and hand bones display features that are distinctly non-avian.
It has been claimed that Protoavis constitutes the oldest known avian taxon, as its fossils date back about 210 million years, much earlier than those of Archaeopteryx.
The holotype and paratype specimens were discovered in 1984 at a quarry in the Texas panhandle within a Triassic river delta sedimentary layer.
The holotype and paratype fossils were found in different locations and were disarticulated and unassociated.
The Protoavis fossils represent a jumbled collection of disarticulated bones resulting from a mass mortality event caused by a flash flood.
Reconstructions depict Protoavis as a carnivorous bird with front-facing eyes, suggesting a nocturnal or crepuscular lifestyle.
The principal carnivores in the environment of Protoavis were poposaurids like Postosuchus.
The postcranial remains are so poorly preserved, or worse, than the cranial elements that Chatterjee's interpretation is in many cases unfounded or speculative.
The quality of vertebral conservation is poor; while the centra are modified, they do not appear to be truly heterocoelous.
The reduction of neural spines is questionable.

Chatterjee's interpretation of fossils identified as such in his reviews of Protoavis material is open to questioning due to the preservation quality of the elements, and it is currently unclear if any of the characters were actually present in Protoavis.
The coracoid, identified by Chatterjee as keeled and retroverted, is, like the supposed furcula and sternum, too poorly preserved to allow precise identification.

The supposed fusion of the ischium and ilium into an ilioischial plate is not currently corroborated by the fossils in question, despite Chatterjee's auspicious illustration to the contrary in The Rise of Birds.

At this time, the pelvic girdle is not well enough preserved to determine if there was or was not a renal fossa, although since no known Mesozoic bird presents a renal fossa, it is unclear why Protoavis should, even if it is more derived than Archaeopteryx.
The metacarpian structures appear to be attributable to post-mortem damage.
After a more detailed examination of the material, no structures homologous to remige papillae were isolated.
The genus Protoavis was originally named by Talbot in 1911 and redefined by Chatterjee in 1984.
Protoavis is classified within the parent group Theropoda and in the class Reptilia.
Protoavis lived during the Late Triassic period, and the Dockum Group, where fossils were found, dates from the Carnian to the early Norian stages of the terminal Triassic.
The paleoclimate of the Dockum Group was subtropical with a distinct dry and wet season pattern marked by monsoonal rains.

The true classification of Protoavis is controversial with many different interpretations of what the animal actually is. If the identification of Protoavis as a bird is valid, it would push back the origins of birds by 60 to 75 million years. Many paleontologists doubt that Protoavis is a bird or that all remains come from a single species due to unconvincing avian features in the fragmentary material. Data suggest that prokinesis in the skull of Protoavis is questionable and that the specimen likely displays a conventional opisthostylic quadrate. The presence of poorly developed hypapophyses on non-avian vertebrae is regarded as mild convergence rather than evidence of avian affinity. Researchers question whether the pectoral girdle features described by Chatterjee were actually present in Protoavis because the fossil preservation is poor.
